extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of Popular Science Monthly; readers interested in philosophy of religion, ethics, and evolution (late 19th-century scientific and theological readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science / philosophical essay arguing how the phenomenon of conscience can be accounted for by evolutionary processes, defining key features of conscience and sketching stages in its development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience is instantaneous in origin (innate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience is instantaneous — that is, innate — in its origin, and therefore not to be accounted for by the supposition that by degrees it was impressed upon the mind from without. It bears so strong a resemblance to the other faculties, the senses and emotions, that, like them, it must have formed part of the original constitution of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for any explanation of conscience: it must allow for conscience to appear as a non-composite, immediate faculty (coeval with self-consciousness) rather than solely as the slow accumulation of experiences or external impressions. Explanatory accounts should show how evolutionary processes can yield such an apparently 'instantaneous' faculty at a critical epoch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience is instantaneous in operation (intuitional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience is instantaneous — that is, intuitional — in its operations, and therefore not to be accounted for by the action and reaction of social relationships. Had there been but one man, that one man would have been able to say, 'I must do this.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable accounts must explain how conscience can function as an immediate perception of rightness (like perception by the eye) even in the absence of society; the theory should account for a direct correlation between conscience and an external 'rightness' rather than reducing conscience to only social/utility-based reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience is instantaneous in command (imperative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience is also instantaneous — that is, imperative — in its commands. It never stops to argue when once the right is, or is thought to be, ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory explanation must account for the felt obligatoriness of conscience (its immediate imperative force) rather than treating 'ought' as merely a residual product of a gradual utility-calculation; explanations should address why no archaeological 'ladder' traces of developing 'ought' are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience defined as the power of discerning rightness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience is merely the power which the mind possesses of discerning rightness. Just as we discern something called 'beautiful' which we must admire, or something 'pleasurable' which we must seek, so do we perceive something 'right' which we must do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating theories of moral origin, treat 'conscience' as the cognitive-perceptual capacity to detect rightness; focus inquiry on how the idea or fact of rightness entered cognitive life rather than on theological labels. Explanations should connect perceptual/cognitive processes to moral judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory accounts must reproduce the apparent 'instantaneousness'
rubrics_metrics.description: If evolution can be proved to account precisely for those phenomena that seem prima facie to militate most strongly against it (the instantaneous/innate/intuitional/imperative aspects), then evolution is confirmed for explaining conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation standard: an evolutionary account should show how critical unions of conditions (e.g., self-consciousness + environmental pressures) can produce qualitatively new faculties 'instantaneously' in experience, analogous to poetic 'creation' phrases; use natural-selection narratives and the emergence of self-awareness to justify sudden-appearing moral perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast (perception of dissimilarities) as necessary condition for moral knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition essential to all knowledge, namely, contrast or the perception of dissimilarities, is present: 'As light is meaningless without darkness, or heat without cold, so is right without its contrast of force or wrong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any account of the origin of moral sense should rest on the cognitive capacity to perceive contrasts (threat vs. safety, self-preservation vs. destruction); show how such contrasts yield affective responses that become the seeds of moral discernment and vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal-stage materials as raw elements for conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: The Animal Stage: the materials out of which conscience has been constructed are discernible in animal life — instincts like flight, combination for defense, appealing looks, cries of remonstrance, self-defense to the last moment — and these, with the touch of self-consciousness, become the germ of conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for plausibility: show continuity from animal instincts and emotions to human conscience; explanatory models should demonstrate how pre-existing animal behaviors and affective states could be transformed by self-consciousness into moral perception and obligation (the 'rough unhewed stones' becoming moral faculties).
